title: TESS sector 82 shows a second transit of the Kepler single-transit candidate KIC 10284575; Kepler and TESS data permit only six periods from 712 to 4983 days
abstract: Many long-period planet candidates in Kepler data have only one transit, so their period is not known. TESS observed the Kepler field again in 2019-2024 (sectors 14-83). We searched TESS light curves (SPOC, TESS-SPOC, QLP and own TESScut photometry for 364 slots without a pipeline light curve) of 80 Kepler stars with single-transit or double-transit candidates from four catalogues (Kawahara & Masuda 2019; Foreman-Mackey et al. 2016; Uehara et al. 2016; Herman et al. 2019). We used Kepler-fitted trapezoid templates, a noise-calibrated matched filter, a Gaia-based dilution model and 4524 injections. KIC 10284575 (KOI-3210, Tmag 11.6) shows a second transit on 2024-09-03 with the same depth (0.50-0.58%) and duration (25.7 +- 0.7 h) as its Kepler event of 2011-01-12. Aperture, sky, comparison-star and difference-image tests put the flux loss on the target, and the Kepler centroid puts the source within about 1 arcsec. Kepler and TESS coverage reject all periods 4983.43/n except n = 1-5 and 7 (4983, 2492, 1661, 1246, 997 and 712 d). The companion radius is 1.07 R_Jup; it can be a temperate giant planet, a brown dwarf or a low-mass star. TESS also shows no transit at the epoch that the published 494.44-d period of Kepler-1704 b predicts (9.4 sigma), in agreement with its 988.88-d RV period. Over all single-transit candidates, TESS had SNR >= 10 sensitivity to the Kepler depth for only 3 of 51 stars. The published period estimates predict 0.19 (KM19), 0.49 (H19), 0.14 (FM16) and 0.00 (U16) TESS detections; we found 1 (KIC 10284575, a KM19 entry). This agrees with the estimates but has low power. Limitations: the TESS event occurs during scattered light at the end of a sector and only QLP and own photometry cover it; the companion mass is unknown; the dilution model is approximate.

display.caption: KIC 10284575: Kepler quarter 8 event (left) and the TESS sector 82 event 4983.4 d later in own TESScut photometry (centre) and QLP (right). Red: 0.55%, 25-h trapezoid.

Checks on the TESS event: comparison stars, sky level, depth against aperture size and sky method (S82 event constant; sector-55 edge dips behave as sky errors), and the difference image with Gaia DR3 stars.
Why TESS could test few candidates: depth against TESS magnitude coloured by sensitive fraction (A), injection-recovery efficiency (B), and per-entry probability of a detectable TESS transit (C).
